# Ēl, spelled the way the sources wrote it
There is a version of this name the early internet had to settle for: *el*. This is the file on how **Ēl** replaced it.

Ēl appears in almost every major Ugaritic myth, yet he rarely takes center stage. He is the one appealed to, the one who gives or withholds blessing, the one whose laughter signals cosmic assent. His mythology is the mythology of authority itself — distant, benevolent, sometimes foolish, always final. In KTU 1. 2 iii, Ēl initially grants kingship to Yamm, the Sea.

That is the figure this file is about — and the temple now standing at its restored name.
## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Ēl
- **ASCII form:** el
- **Meaning:** "The high god of the Canaanite pantheon; the common Semitic word for "god" and a divine name"
- **Domain of influence:** Supreme God, Father of Gods
- **Pantheon:** Canaanite
- **Classification:** Tier 1
- **Original script:** 𐎛𐎍
- **Series:** The Restoration Files, No. 74 of 271
## The Name Before the Marks

The name is attested as **Ἠλ**. On the evidence, it means "The high god of the Canaanite pantheon; the common Semitic word for "god" and a divine name".

Strip **Ēl** to *el* and one piece of evidence vanishes:

- **e → Ē** — Macron marks long /ē/; capitalized in the restoration: the vowel length the ASCII form cannot show.

A reader who knows the marks hears the name correctly on the first try. A reader who never sees them never gets the chance.
## The Temple That Stands Now

The restored name is not a plaque; it is an address. The temple of **Ēl** lives at [/sites/el/](/sites/el/), with its mythology in the [lore halls](/sites/el/lore/), its peer-reviewed record in the [Scholarly Edition](/sites/el/scholars/), and its place in the pattern atlas on the [patterns floor](/sites/el/patterns/).

The restoration preserves more than the ASCII form can say — stress, length, or a letter the Latin keyboard lost — which places it in Tier-1: mechanically verifiable, information-rich.

Every flagship temple is hand-built to the same standard: the original script displayed with its provenance, the pronunciation reconstructed phoneme by phoneme, the sources named — because a restoration you cannot audit is just a spelling with confidence.
## The Archetype at Work

A temple is also a reading of what this figure *means* — and meanings have addresses in the modern world. The [pattern atlas](/patterns/) maps **Ēl** to the industries its archetype genuinely resonates with, each match argued, weighted, and open to challenge:

- **Leadership, Governance & Public Administration** — The father of gods; the patriarchal template of rule.
- **Faith & Spiritual Organizations** — The ancient Semitic god-name still embedded in living liturgy.
- **Ancestry & Heritage Services** — Father of gods and ‘father of years’; the patriarch at the head of the oldest divine family tree.

The mapping is conservative on purpose: only resonances that can be argued aloud. The rest of the atlas follows the same rule, industry by industry.
## In the Sacred Texts

The Canaanite tradition is not a vibe; it is a library. The [Sacred Texts collection](/texts/) holds [Enūma Eliš](/texts/enuma-elish/) — the primary sources the temple's scholarship is built on, free to read, cross-linked back to the names they mention. The temple is the argument; the texts are the evidence.
